sjt.scenario: Two vice presidents each ask you for a piece of urgent work, both due by 5pm today. You realistically have time to do one of them well.
options: Do the work for the more senior of the two and tell the other one later that you ran out of time.
Tell both of them straight away about the clash, give an honest estimate for each, and ask them (or your manager) to agree which comes first.
Rush both pieces so that you hit both deadlines.
Do the task you find easier first, then start the other if there is time.

sjt.scenario: You notice that a revenue figure in a presentation your team sent to a client yesterday was double-counted. Nobody else seems to have spotted it.
options: Tell the associate on the deal straight away, showing the correct figure and where it comes from.
Correct the figure in the internal file so future versions are right, without mentioning it.
Wait to see whether the client notices.
Email the client directly with the corrected figure.

sjt.scenario: You are working on a group project with three other interns. One of them has missed two team check-ins and has not started their section, which is due in three days.
options: Quietly do their section yourself so the project is finished on time.
Speak to them privately, ask what is going on, and agree what they will deliver and by when.
Raise it with the programme manager straight away.
Mention it in the group chat so the whole team knows what is happening.

sjt.scenario: A client calls and asks you for information about another deal your team is working on. You are not sure whether you are allowed to share it.
options: Share what you know, because keeping the client happy is the priority.
Tell the client you will check and come back to them today, then ask your manager or compliance.
Refuse firmly and end the call.
Give a vague answer so the client does not feel brushed off.

sjt.scenario: In your mid-internship review, your manager says your attention to detail needs to improve.
options: Ask for specific examples, agree a plan to improve, and ask to check in again in two weeks.
Explain why the mistakes were not really your fault.
Accept it without discussion and start working longer hours to double-check everything.
Ask the other interns whether they received the same feedback.

verbal.text: When central bank rates rise, bank margins usually widen at first.
verbal.passage: Net interest margin measures the difference between the interest a bank earns on its loans and the interest it pays on deposits, expressed as a percentage of its interest-earning assets. When central bank rates rise, banks can usually increase the rates they charge on new loans faster than they raise the rates paid to savers, so margins tend to widen at first. This effect rarely lasts. As savers move money into higher-paying fixed-term accounts, the cost of deposits catches up, and competition for borrowers puts pressure on lending rates. Analysts therefore watch the “deposit beta”, the share of a central bank rate rise that is passed on to depositors, as an early sign of where margins are heading. A bank with a large base of current accounts, which typically pay little or no interest, is usually less exposed to rising deposit costs than one that relies on savings accounts and wholesale funding.

verbal.text: Money from a sustainability-linked loan must be spent on an environmental project.
verbal.passage: Unlike a green loan, where the money must be spent on a specific environmental project, a sustainability-linked loan can be used for general corporate purposes. Instead, its interest rate is tied to the borrower meeting agreed sustainability targets, such as cutting carbon emissions by a set percentage. If the targets are met, the margin falls, typically by a small amount such as 0.05 percentage points; if they are missed, it may rise by a similar amount. Critics argue that some targets have been set too low to be meaningful, which has led lenders to ask for independent verification of borrowers’ performance. Supporters respond that even a small change in borrowing costs focuses senior management’s attention, because the targets are disclosed publicly and missing them carries a reputational cost.

group.title: Harbour & Co: where should a coffee chain invest?
group.brief: Harbour & Co runs 210 coffee shops in the South of England. Revenue £180m, operating margin 9%. The board has £40m to invest and wants one recommendation from your group in 20 minutes.

options.name: A. Buy Northern Bean (60 cafés, Manchester and Leeds)
options.facts: Price £35m. Revenue £38m, margin 6% (Harbour thinks it can reach 9% in 3 years). Brand is weaker; 12 sites have leases ending within 2 years.

options.name: B. Open 25 drive-thru sites
options.facts: Cost £25m over 3 years (£1m each). Each site expected to make £1.4m revenue at 14% margin once mature (about 18 months). Planning permission is uncertain for a third of sites.

options.name: C. Launch a supermarket coffee range
options.facts: Cost £15m (product, packaging, marketing). Two supermarkets interested. Forecast revenue £20m by year 3 at 11% margin. Supermarkets can drop ranges at 3 months’ notice.
